courses.description: Students will explore and engage with an array of literature from around the world, and develop an understanding of the richness of global diversity through a study of some of the world’s finest literature. Students will read and respond to works of fiction through a variety of modes, including written essays, presentations, artistic representations, debates and more. Whenever possible, our study will complement the Global Studies curriculum. Upon completion of this class, students will have an understanding of many works of World Literature and be ready to dive deeper into another aspect of the discipline.
courses.notes: Objective: To compare and contrast in writing and through discussion, understand the literary elements and essential concepts, and write formal and informal assignments that utilize all stages of the writing process.

courses.description: This interdisciplinary course meets during two blocks: one with an English teacher and one with a Social Studies teacher, who work together to blend the curriculum and skills from both departments. Students begin with an exploration of the Paleolithic Era and the development of the first civilizations, including study of some of the earliest written literature. Students continue with an examination of classical societies: tracing the expansion of trade networks and their global impact, emphasizing the role of belief systems and shifts in political power, and developing an understanding of the universal themes and symbols common to literary works from around the world. Students will have the opportunity to engage with a wide range of literary forms, historical themes, cultures, and periods while building reading and writing skills to meet English and Global Citizenship proficiencies.
courses.notes: Objective: To develop an understanding of a variety of cultural experiences, historical events and perspectives through the study of literary works and historical materials. To compare and contrast, in writing and through discussion, and demonstrate an understanding of the personalities, trends, and beliefs that have shaped various histories and cultures from around the world.; Interdisciplinary course meeting two blocks (English and Social Studies teachers)

courses.description: Students will read and analyze works of American literature from pre-colonial Native American mythology, colonial, 19th century, 20th century, to contemporary times, including poetry, short stories, novels, drama, and nonfiction. Students will continue to hone independent reading skills and be prepared to complete analytical assignments outside of class. One of our primary goals will be to move beyond a reader response approach to literature into deep analysis. Students will be encouraged to develop their own interpretations to literature that are well supported by specific evidence from the text.
courses.notes: Objective: To compare and contrast the literary elements in writing and through discussion, and demonstrate an understanding of personalities, trends and beliefs that have shaped American history and culture.; Catalog lists "American Literature I and II" as one entry with a shared description

courses.description: Students will read and analyze works of American literature from pre-colonial Native American mythology, colonial, 19th century, 20th century, to contemporary times, including poetry, short stories, novels, drama, and nonfiction. Students will continue to hone independent reading skills and be prepared to complete analytical assignments outside of class. One of our primary goals will be to move beyond a reader response approach to literature into deep analysis. Students will be encouraged to develop their own interpretations to literature that are well supported by specific evidence from the text.
courses.notes: Objective: To compare and contrast the literary elements in writing and through discussion, and demonstrate an understanding of personalities, trends and beliefs that have shaped American history and culture.; Catalog lists "American Literature I and II" as one entry with a shared description

courses.description: This interdisciplinary course pairing meets during two blocks, one with an English teacher and one with a Social Studies teacher, who work together to blend the curriculum and skills from both departments. This course examines the significant chapters of American society through a historical and literary lens. This course explores and engages with a wide array of literature. Focusing on a key decade in American life—the 1890s, for example, or the 1950s—this course will examine the dynamics of race, class, gender, and ethnicity as forces that have shaped, and been shaped by, American culture. Why did some groups achieve hegemony and not others, and what were—and are—the implications of these dynamics for our understanding of American culture?
courses.notes: Objective: To connect U.S. history to American literature and gain a solid understanding of American Literature, rhetoric, and history. This course is designed to prepare students for AP Language and Composition and/or AP U.S. History.; Interdisciplinary course meeting two blocks (English and Social Studies teachers)

courses.description: With an emphasis on continuing to strengthen foundational skills and knowledge, this course builds on the skills learned in World Literature. Texts may include memoir, short story and novels; and the craft of analytic essays will be the majority of the writing focus.
courses.notes: Objective: To improve reading comprehension, writing mechanics, verbal communication, and listening comprehension.; Grade level as printed: Intended Grade Level: 9-12, with teacher recommendation

courses.description: The Vermont Experience (TVE) course focuses on helping students improve and grow their reading, writing, and analytical skills using content created by local writers, musicians, and artists who focus on the natural world and environment. Content includes, but is not limited to, plants, animals, forests, landscapes, and crops of Vermont. Students can expect to read, write, and analyze every day and will evidence their learning in a digital portfolio structured and organized by WRVSU’s Proficiencies for English Language Arts. Students can also expect to spend significant time outdoors regardless of the season. TVE is a project-centered, pass/fail course. Students who pass TVE earn one credit of English towards their graduation requirements. Students pass TVE through biweekly assessments of their portfolios.
courses.fulfills_text: Students who pass TVE earn one credit of English towards their graduation requirements.
courses.notes: Objective: To improve reading, writing, and analytical skills.

courses.description: This course is designed to study the short story as an art form. Students are expected to engage actively with the reading through class discussions and written responses. In addition to developing critical reading skills, this course helps students learn to recognize, appreciate, and react to a variety of writing styles. Authors studied may include Edgar Allan Poe, Anton Chekhov, Charlotte Perkins Gilman, James Baldwin, Ernest Hemingway, William Faulkner, Flannery O'Connor, John Cheever, Raymond Carver, and Alice Walker, Louise Erdrich, and Sherman Alexie among others. Assessments include standard literary analysis essays as well as reading journals and creative projects. Students will also explore a single author through a multi-faceted independent project.
courses.notes: Objective: To read texts from various genres and to analyze and understand the implications, elements, and underlying questions of the text via the author's craft.

courses.description: This course offers students a supportive workshop environment to develop their writing skills and provides them with experience in various forms of imaginative writing. Students take individual responsibility for their own writing, for their use of class time, and for helping each other at all stages of the writing process. The teacher directs the class as a facilitator, helping the students to develop into a community of independent writers. Students will study writing samples from professional writers as well as student writers to guide student progress.
courses.credits_text: Half year (0.5 Credit) and can take both for 1 Credit
courses.notes: Objective: To examine the works of published writers as well as their peers to discover, expand, and refine their own skills, voice, and repertoire.; Grade level as printed: Intended Grade Level: 9-12 (For 9th graders, must be taken concurrently with either World Literature or Honors World Studies: Literature); Length/credit as printed: Half year (0.5 Credit) and can take both for 1 Credit; Catalog lists "Creative Writing I and II" as one entry with a shared description

courses.description: Students in this class read a selection of the comedies, tragedies, histories, and other scripts. Students engage in dramatic readings of plays, closely examine and analyze language and structure, experiment with stagecraft, and explore the process of taking works from the page to the stage.
courses.notes: Objective: To compare and contrast interpretations, engage in discussion, and demonstrate an understanding of works written for the theatrical stage.

courses.description: In this class, students read a selection of poetry from around the world and write their own works of poetry. Students engage in varied writing exercises, closely examine and analyze language and structure, experiment with sharing our work, and explore the ways that poetic forms can communicate and express our experiences with the world.
courses.notes: Objective: To express, understand and examine the poetic form, through readings, discussions, and to create a body of poetic work.

courses.course_name: Rhetoric: The Art of Persuasive Writing and Public Speaking
courses.description: The focus is on learning to construct and defend compelling arguments. Students will engage in civil discourse as they investigate rhetoric and its impact on culture through analysis of notable fiction and nonfiction texts, from pamphlets to speeches to personal essays. Through this analysis, students learn how speakers and writers persuade an audience to adopt their point of view. Students continue to develop more precise writing skills and write literary analysis, arguments, and narrative pieces, focusing on the skills of topic development, organization, diction/syntax, and the use of textual evidence. Grammar is reviewed through writing to emphasize the finer points of mechanics and word choice, and vocabulary is drawn from both the readings and from other sources. Students prepare for and participate effectively in a range of conversations to express their ideas and learn from/build on the ideas of others.
courses.notes: Objective: To introduce the theory and practice of rhetoric, the art of persuasive writing and speech, and the value of informed citizenship.

courses.description: This lab will provide supplemental instruction to support core writing courses or specific writing projects. We will emphasize the writing process: outlining, drafting, revising, and editing, through workshops and individualized feedback. Labs must be taken concurrently
courses.notes: Objective: Labs must be taken concurrently with another English class and are graded as pass/fail. To reinforce fundamental English skills in writing and reading through basic grammar, vocabulary building, and simple composition exercises.; Must be taken concurrently with another English class; graded pass/fail

courses.description: This lab will provide supplemental instruction to support core writing courses or specific writing projects. We will emphasize the writing process, outlining, drafting, revising, and editing, through workshops and individualized feedback.
courses.notes: Objective: Labs must be taken concurrently with another English class and are graded as pass/fail. To reinforce fundamental English skills in writing and reading through basic grammar, vocabulary building, and simple composition exercises.; Must be taken concurrently with another English class; graded pass/fail

courses.description: In this course, students focus on the development of a single literary form throughout a specific time period, genre, or cultural study. Students are introduced to the intellectual and literary movements associated with the topic and engage in deep analysis of these literary concepts through a variety of modes. Writing assignments include expository, analytical, and argumentative essays that require students to analyze and interpret literary works. This is a rotating course, based on student need and class enrollment. Past selections have included: Horror, British Literature, Seminar in American Literature and Seminar in World Literature.
courses.offering_note: Rotating course, based on student need and class enrollment
courses.notes: Objective: To develop student understanding of a variety of experiences and perspectives, focusing on a particular topic related to literature, film, and other forms of cultural studies.

courses.description: This co-taught course will cover journalism fundamentals: expository writing, interviewing techniques, editing, photography, and digital design. It requires strong teamwork to manage content, layout, and to adhere to strict deadlines.
courses.notes: Objective: To produce a regularly published newspaper (print/online).; Grade level as printed: Intended Grade Level: 9-12 (For 9th graders, must be taken concurrently with either World Literature or Honors World Studies: Literature)

courses.description: This course guides students in becoming curious, critical, and responsive readers of diverse texts, and becoming flexible, reflective writers of texts addressed to diverse audiences for diverse purposes. The course cultivates the rhetorical understanding and use of written language by directing students’ attention to writer/reader interactions in their reading and writing of various formal and informal genres. Reading and writing activities in the course also deepen students’ knowledge and control of formal conventions of written language (Ex: vocabulary, diction, syntax, spelling, punctuation, paragraphing, genre). Course readings facilitate informed citizenship and thus increase students’ capacity to enter into consequential conversations after evaluating sources from all sides of a meaningful issue. Students will build awareness of a writer’s purposes, audience expectations, and subjects, as well as the way conventions and the resources of language contribute to effectiveness in writing. All students are required to take the AP exam.
courses.prerequisites: None, however it is recommended that students have taken Global Studies and American Studies. They should be able to read and comprehend college-level texts and write grammatically correct, complete sentences.
courses.notes: Objective: To focus on critical literacy, facilitating informed citizenship, and interactions among a writer’s purpose, audience, and subjects, as well as the way genre conventions and the resources of language contribute to effectiveness in writing.

courses.description: In this course, students devote themselves to the study of literary works written in, or translated into, English. Careful reading and critical analysis of such works of fiction, drama, and poetry, selected locally by responsible educators, provide rich opportunities for students to develop an appreciation of ways literature reflects and comments on a range of experiences, institutions, and social structures. Students will examine the choices literary writers make and the techniques they utilize to achieve purposes and generate meanings. As they read, students consider a work’s structure, style, and themes, as well as its use of figurative language, imagery, and symbolism. Writing assignments include expository, analytical, and argumentative essays that require students to analyze and interpret literary works. This course aligns to an introductory college-level literature and writing curriculum. All students are required to take the AP exam.
courses.prerequisites: None, however students should be able to read and comprehend college-level texts and write grammatically correct, complete sentences.
courses.notes: Objective: To engage in close reading and critical analysis of imaginative literature (Ex: fiction, poetry, drama) from various time periods, to deepen their understanding of the ways writers use language to provide meaning.

courses.description: This course will provide a solid foundation of various mathematics skills and concepts so that students can prepare for Algebra 1. The concepts covered will include fractions, decimals, irrational numbers, algebraic expressions, algebraic properties, solving algebraic equations, introduction to functions, square roots, three-dimensional geometry, angles, slope and lines.
courses.prerequisites: Teacher recommendation
courses.notes: Objective: To build an understanding of algebraic expressions, equations, and functions.

courses.description: This course will begin with a review of Pre-Algebra concepts, including working with variable expressions, integers and rational numbers, like terms, problem-solving strategies, and the distributive property. The course is intended to build a conceptual understanding of basic algebra using guided practice. Topics include: solving linear equations and inequalities; working with variables, expressions, and formulas; graphing, writing and interpreting linear functions; understanding slope and rate of change; systems of equations; and introductory work with polynomials and exponents.
courses.prerequisites: 8th Grade Math or Pre-Algebra with teacher recommendation
courses.notes: Objective: To broaden knowledge of the fundamentals of algebra.

courses.description: The emphasis of this section of this course will be on the utilization of algebraic models to solve practical problems. This course offers the fundamentals of algebra. Topics covered will include understanding variables and algebraic expressions, solving single variable linear expressions, graphing linear equations, writing and using linear models to solve problems, understanding functions, solving systems of linear equations and inequalities, graphing and writing linear inequalities, understanding exponential rules, graphing and writing exponential equations, and analyzing data using probability and statistics. Other topics may include quadratic models, solving quadratic equations, using operations with polynomials, and factoring.
courses.prerequisites: 8th Grade Math or Pre-Algebra with teacher recommendation
courses.notes: Objective: To build a strong and logical algebra foundation essential to study math and science at the upper level.

courses.description: Students enrolled in this honors level course are expected to work independently, complete higher level assignments, and complete enrichment projects outside of the classroom. This course is for students with a strong mathematical background, the ability to work independently, and, have shown a readiness for advanced problem solving. This course emphasizes critical thinking, analytical reasoning, and mathematical communication. Topics include: solving and analyzing linear equations and inequalities; writing, graphing, and interpreting linear functions; systems of equations and inequalities; operations with polynomials and factoring; exponents and exponential functions; introductory quadratic functions and equations.
courses.prerequisites: 8th Grade Math or Pre-Algebra with teacher recommendation
courses.notes: Objective: To extend knowledge beyond the fundamentals of algebra essential to study math and science at the upper level.

courses.description: This course is designed for students who would benefit from a class that has additional algebra skill reinforcement such as solving one-step equations, multistep equations, ratios, proportions, and equations with fractions while building a conceptual understanding of geometry. There will be an emphasis on learning and applying geometry concepts through hands-on activities that help reinforce the learning. Topics in geometry will include applications in: segment and angle addition, angle pair relationships, congruence, classifications of triangles and quadrilaterals, Pythagorean Theorem, area, volume, and surface area. Other topics may include Trigonometry concepts.
courses.prerequisites: Algebra I, and students who took Algebra I in 8th grade must also get teacher recommendation
courses.notes: Objective: To broaden knowledge of the fundamentals of geometry.

courses.description: The emphasis of this section of geometry will be on the understanding of geometric terminology, formulas, and relationships. Although logical deductive proofs will be covered, there will not be an emphasis on these. Geometry is about measuring, understanding the properties, shapes and relationships of the physical world. It is closely connected with other branches of mathematics, such as algebra, logic, probability, and trigonometry. Understanding the logical structure of geometry is important to the students’ success in this course. They will learn what it means to define a term, test a conjecture, and prove a theorem. After taking this course, the students’ ability to see geometry in their surroundings should improve, such as recognition of patterns, shapes, sizes, illusions, and similarities.
courses.prerequisites: Algebra I, and students who took Algebra I in 8th grade must also get teacher recommendation
courses.notes: Objective: To build a strong and logical geometry foundation essential to study math and science at the upper level.

courses.description: Students enrolled in this honors level course are expected to work independently, complete higher level assignments, and complete enrichment projects outside of the classroom.This course is for students with a strong mathematical background, the ability to work independently, and, have shown a readiness for advanced problem solving. This course emphasizes critical thinking, analytical reasoning, and mathematical communication. Topics include the regular content of Geometry. Extra topics may include: completing the square to find the center and radius of a circle; logic and Venn Diagrams; in depth relationships with triangles and quadrilaterals; applications of the Pythagorean Theorem and special triangles; Law of Cosines and Sines with applications of trigonometry; literal equations involving volume and surface area; pi and radians; and chords, secants, and tangents of a circle.
courses.prerequisites: Algebra I, and students who took Algebra I in 8th grade must also get teacher recommendation
courses.notes: Objective: To extend knowledge beyond the fundamentals of geometry essential to study math and science at the upper level.

courses.description: This course will begin with a review of Algebra 1 concepts, such as solving one-variable equations, and graphing linear equations and inequalities. The course is intended to strengthen a conceptual understanding of algebra using guided practice. Topics will include exponential and quadratic expressions and functions. Other topics may include complex numbers, rational and radical expressions, and polynomial functions.
courses.prerequisites: Algebra I, Geometry, and teacher recommendation
courses.notes: Objective: To broaden knowledge of algebra by expanding on prior knowledge of functions and relations.

courses.description: This course is more deeply involved with some of the ideas of Algebra 1. Expressions and functions, such as linear, exponential, quadratic functions, polynomial, rational, radical, and logarithmic are explored. Other topics include inequalities, linear systems of equations, complex numbers, polynomial operations, composite functions, modeling, and identifying key features of graphs.
courses.prerequisites: Algebra 1, Geometry, and teacher recommendation
courses.notes: Objective: To build a strong and logical Algebra II foundation essential to study math and science at the upper level.

courses.description: This course is designed to prepare students for AP Pre-Calculus. Students enrolled in this honors level course are expected to work independently, complete higher level assignments, and complete enrichment projects outside of the classroom. This course is for students with a strong mathematical background, the ability to work independently, and, have shown a readiness for advanced problem solving. This course takes a deeper dive into understanding and modeling functions; including linear, exponential, quadratic functions, polynomial, rational, radical, and logarithmic. Other topics include inequalities, systems of equations, complex numbers, polynomial operations, and composite functions.
courses.prerequisites: Algebra I Honors, Geometry Honors, or Algebra I and Geometry, with teacher recommendation
courses.notes: Objective: To extend knowledge beyond the fundamentals of Algebra II essential to study math and science at the upper level.

courses.description: Students will pursue the work of statistical concepts including understanding categorical and quantitative data, observational studies and experiments, sampling, probability, probability models, and modeling linear and curved relationships between two variables. Additional topics include confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, interpreting data, and inferences. Graphing calculators and computer applications will be used to observe and model data.
courses.prerequisites: Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II
courses.notes: Objective: To gain a strong understanding of the concepts of statistics.

courses.description: This course offers a rigorous study of the fundamentals of Pre-Calculus. This course prepares students for AP Calculus AB or college Calculus. Content will focus on the three units required by the College Board (Polynomial & Rational Functions, Exponential & Logarithmic Functions, and Trigonometric & Polar Functions.) If time allows, content will also include the optional fourth unit (Functions Involving Parameters, Vectors, and Matrices.) This expands on the content taught in Algebra II Honors. Students will prepare for the Advanced Placement examination, which is prepared and scored by the College Board. Qualifying grades may allow a student to receive credit and advanced standing on a college level. Students should expect to commit a significant amount of time to ensure completion of the required content. The use of the graphing calculator is required on the AP examination; therefore, students are required to have their own graphing calculator. All students are required to take the AP exam.
courses.prerequisites: Algebra I/Algebra I Honors, Geometry/Geometry Honors, Algebra II Honors
courses.notes: Objective: Students will learn and apply the concepts of a college level Pre-Calculus course. including topics of limits, differentiation and integration. Depending on the institution of interest, students may have the opportunity to receive college credit if successful with a score of 4 or 5 on the national AP exam.

courses.description: Students will pursue the work of calculus on a level equivalent to that found in a college Calculus I course. Students will prepare for the Advanced Placement examination, which is prepared and scored by the College Board. Qualifying grades may allow a student to receive credit and advanced standing on a college level. Students should expect to commit a significant amount of time to ensure completion of the required content. The use of the graphing calculator is required on the AP examination; therefore, students are required to have their own graphing calculator. All students are required to take the AP exam.
courses.prerequisites: Algebra I/Algebra I Honors, Geometry/Geometry Honors, Algebra II Honors, AP Pre-Calculus
courses.notes: Objective: The student will be able to work with functions in a variety of ways, including graphical, numerical, analytic, and verbal. Students will learn and apply the concepts of a college level Calculus I course, including topics of limits, differentiation and integration. Depending on the institution of interest, students may have the opportunity to receive college credit if successful with a score of 4 or 5 on the national AP exam.

courses.description: Students will explore physics through the science and engineering practices as they consider real-world applications and physical processes on Earth and in space. Though we will engage in all the science practices, particular emphasis will be placed on designing and conducting experiments, working with quantitative data, and constructing evidence-based explanations. Topics covered include forces and how they impact motion, collisions and how to reduce impact force in a collision, waves and how we use waves in technology today, the transfer and generation of electric charge, and the movement and transformation of energy.
courses.notes: Objective: Students will practice and apply the science practices to help them make sense of the physical world.

courses.description: Students in Honors Conceptual Physics will be expected to explore conceptual physics concepts in depth, utilize texts, data, and models, and express their learning in a variety of writing formats. Students will explore physics through the science and engineering practices as they consider real-world applications and physical processes on Earth and in space. Though we will engage in all the science practices, particular emphasis will be placed on designing and conducting experiments, working with quantitative data, and constructing evidence-based explanations. Topics covered include forces and how they impact motion, collisions and how to reduce impact force in a collision, waves and how we use waves in technology today, the transfer and generation of electric charge, and the movement and transformation of energy.
courses.notes: Objective: Students will practice and apply the science practices to help them make sense of the physical world.

courses.description: This class will be taught in close collaboration with the math department in order to provide additional math support. Students will explore Physics concepts in a supported and scaffolded classroom environment through hands-on learning experiences, while learning and practicing foundational math skills. Topics covered include measurement and graphing of data, motion and forces, gravity, collisions, energy, waves, and the transfer and interactions of electric charges.
courses.notes: Objective: Students will develop and practice foundational skills in the areas of science and engineering and math while engaging in hands-on learning experiences to help them make sense of the physical world.; Grade level as printed: Intended Grade Level: 9th grade students concurrently taking Transitional Math or Pre-Algebra

courses.description: We will explore the fundamentals of life science through the lens of understanding natural phenomena. We will explore “how life works” through engaging in all of the NGSS science practices, but we will focus specifically on explaining using evidence, analyzing and interpreting data, and modeling. From molecules and cells, to evolution and ecology, we will explore how groups of living organisms survive, interact, reproduce, evolve, and adapt.
courses.prerequisites: Conceptual Physics
courses.notes: Objective: Students will be able to apply the science practices to help them make sense of the science of life.

courses.description: Students in Honors Biology will be expected to explore Biological concepts in depth, utilize texts, data, and models, and express their learning in a variety of writing formats. Honors Biology is designed to prepare students for AP Biology as well as science electives. In this course we will explore the fundamentals of life science through the lens of understanding natural phenomena. We will explore “how life works” through engaging in all of the NGSS science practices, but we will focus specifically on explaining using evidence, analyzing and interpreting data, and modeling. From molecules and cells, to evolution and ecology, we will explore how groups of living organisms survive, interact, reproduce, evolve, and adapt.
courses.prerequisites: Conceptual Physics
courses.notes: Objective: Students will be able to apply the science practices to help them make sense of the science of life.

courses.description: This course covers all of the major topics of chemistry with additional math support. We will talk about matter and what happens at the molecular level. Students will work in the lab and will refine science and engineering practices.
courses.prerequisites: Conceptual Physics, Biology
courses.fulfills_text: Students will complete their third required science credit while learning the fundamentals of chemistry.
courses.notes: Objective: Students will complete their third required science credit while learning the fundamentals of chemistry.

courses.description: This course provides students with the basic topics of modern chemistry required to explain many macroscopic (large scale) observations of matter using concepts on the microscopic (atomic and molecular) level. The course covers states and properties of matter, chemical bonding, and chemical reactions. Students will work in the lab and develop science and engineering practices as determined by the Next Generation Science Standards. This course is recommended for students who plan on attending a 4-year college.
courses.prerequisites: Conceptual Physics, Biology, successful completion of Algebra I
courses.notes: Objective: Students will master the fundamental concepts of chemistry needed to predict and explain the properties and behaviors of matter and energy.

courses.description: This honors-level course provides students with the fundamental topics of chemistry required to take additional lab science courses at the college level. The course covers states and properties of matter, chemical bonding, and chemical reactions. It also allows students to develop inquiry and analysis skills and refine lab practices. This course has more lab writeups and scientific writing, required out-of-class work, and analyzing science texts. This is a course for students who plan on taking lab science courses at the college level.
courses.prerequisites: Conceptual Physics, Biology, Successful completion of Algebra I
courses.notes: Objective: Students will master the fundamental concepts of chemistry needed to predict and explain the properties and behaviors of matter and energy.

courses.description: This class is an Algebra-based Physics class that aims to prepare students for college level science. Students will explore topics such as kinematics, forces, energy, momentum, waves, and electromagnetism through conducting investigations and mathematical modeling. Students will develop critical thinking skills, analyze data, and apply algebra/geometry to explain physical phenomena.
courses.prerequisites: 80%+ final grade in Algebra II or teacher recommendation
courses.notes: Objective: Students will utilize mathematical reasoning, laboratory investigations, and modeling to analyze and explain physical phenomena and master the fundamental concepts of physics.

courses.description: This semester-long course is for any student interested in the human body or planning for a career in health careers such as nursing, medicine, sports medicine, physical therapy or physical training. Specific topics and body systems covered in Human Anatomy and Physiology 1 include anatomical terminology, homeostasis and feedback mechanisms and the endocrine system, the skeletal system, the muscular system, the integumentary system, and the nervous system. Students will uncover the structure of body systems and discover how they interact to allow humans to sustain life. We explore how these systems work effectively in health, and how they are dysregulated in disease. Students learn to effectively apply and communicate this information through research projects, presentations, and engaging with data and models. We also apply these concepts to more complex human biological topics such as epidemiology, public health, drug action, addiction, and sports medicine, based on student interest.
courses.prerequisites: Biology or concurrent enrollment in Biology
courses.notes: Objective: Students will be able to identify the major structures of the human body and to apply science concepts to explain the physiology of all the body systems and their interactions.

courses.description: This semester-long course is for any student interested in the human body or planning for a career in health careers such as nursing, medicine, sports medicine, physical therapy or physical training. Specific topics and body systems covered in this class include anatomical terminology, the circulatory system, the respiratory system, the digestive system, the reproductive system, the excretory system, and the immune system. Students will uncover the structure of body systems and discover how they interact to allow humans to sustain life. We explore how these systems work effectively in health, and how they are dysregulated in disease. Students learn to effectively apply and communicate this information through research projects, presentations, and engaging with data and models. We also apply these concepts to more complex human biological topics such as epidemiology, public health, drug action, addiction, and sports medicine, based on student interest.
courses.prerequisites: Biology or concurrent enrollment in Biology
courses.notes: Objective: Students will be able to identify the major structures of the human body and to apply science concepts to explain the physiology of all the body systems and their interactions.

courses.description: This is an elective science class for people who love spending time outdoors in Vermont. Students will learn about Vermont’s native plants and their uses, including agricultural, medicinal, and industrial. We will learn about food systems, riparian zones, and using plants for remediation. Students will study how to propagate and take care of trees, perennials, annuals, and vegetables. Understanding our local ecosystems include studying soils, animals, and the way in which humans use the land.
courses.prerequisites: TBD
courses.notes: Objective: Students will develop naturalist skills as they spend time in their local classroom–right outside the school!--and in the lab.

courses.description: This course is designed for any student interested in deepening their understanding of Biology and developing the strong reasoning and inquiry skills required for advanced Biology courses in college. It is the equivalent of a two-semester introductory college Biology class. The course is thematically organized around five ideas: Evolution, Cellular Processes, Energy and Communication, Genetics and Information Transfer, and Interactions. At least 25% of our time is spent doing inquiry, which includes laboratory work, examining and building models, and exploring data. We welcome all students with a strong foundation and interest in Biology who are willing to work hard to learn new concepts and skills. All students are required to take the AP exam.
courses.prerequisites: Biology, Chemistry or concurrent enrollment in Chemistry
courses.notes: Objective: Students who complete AP Biology will have a strong foundation to take advanced college courses in science.

courses.description: Students will develop their understanding of interrelationships of the natural world through inquiry-based investigations and field work as they explore core concepts of energy transfer, interactions between Earth systems, interactions between different species and the environment, and sustainability. There will be a lot of time spent outdoors in all seasons, so students should be prepared to dress appropriately. All students are required to take the AP exam.
courses.prerequisites: Biology, Chemistry or concurrent enrollment in Chemistry
courses.notes: Objective: Students will be exposed to the full breadth of a college-level introductory environmental science course, which will leave the student with a strong foundation for taking college science courses.

courses.description: This course begins with the Paleolithic Era and the development of the first civilizations, continues with an examination of classical societies, and traces the expansion of trade networks and their global impact. The course emphasizes the key themes of interactions over time, shifts in political power, and the role of belief systems. While the course emphasizes the importance of historical and spatial thinking, all of the global citizenship proficiencies are introduced in the study of global history and geography.
courses.notes: Objective: Explore and study global history and geography, from First Civilizations through 1750 AD.

courses.description: This interdisciplinary course meets during two blocks: One with an English teacher and one with a Social Studies teacher, who work together to blend the curriculum and skills from both departments. Students begin with an exploration of the Paleolithic Era and the development of the first civilizations, including early written language. Students continue with an examination of classical societies: tracing the expansion of trade networks and their global impact, emphasizing the role of belief systems and shifts in political power, and developing an understanding of the universal themes and symbols common to literary works from around the world. Students will have the opportunity to engage with a wide range of literary forms, historical themes, cultures, and periods while building reading and writing skills to advance English and Global Citizenship proficiencies.
courses.notes: Objective: To develop an understanding of a variety of cultural experiences, historical events and perspectives through the study of literary works and historical materials. To compare and contrast, in writing and through discussion, and demonstrate an understanding of the personalities, trends, and beliefs that have shaped various histories and cultures from around the world.; Interdisciplinary course meeting two blocks (English and Social Studies teachers)

courses.description: This course explores topics such as the Enlightenment, the French Revolution, the Industrial Revolution, Imperialism and Decolonization, the World Wars, the Cold War, and Globalization and the Environment. This course is the “modern” counterpart to Global Studies and Geography I.
courses.notes: Objective: Explore and study global history and geography, from 1750 AD to the present day.

courses.description: U.S. History begins with the colonial and constitutional foundations of the United States. Students will explore the causes of the American Revolution, the creation and impact of the Constitution, and early challenges faced by the United States. Students will also examine the causes and impact of Slavery, Westward expansion, and Federalism on American Society. The class will conclude with an examination of the causes of the American Civil and an examination of how the nation confronted the challenges brought on by it. Civics will also be covered as part of this course.
courses.prerequisites: Global Studies and Geography I
courses.fulfills_text: This course fulfills one half of the U.S. History graduation requirement.
courses.notes: Objective: This course will explore the establishment of the United States of America to the Civil War. This course fulfills one half of the U.S. History graduation requirement.

courses.description: U.S. History II begins with the Reconstruction Era following the Civil War. Industrialization, urbanization, and the accompanying problems are examined, along with America’s emergence as a world power, the impact of Two World Wars, and the Cold War. Students explore the expansion of the Federal government, the fight to make the country a more equal place, and the role of the United States in an increasingly globalized and interconnected world. Civics will also be covered as part of this course.
courses.prerequisites: Global Studies and Geography, U.S. History I
courses.fulfills_text: This course fulfills one half of the U.S. History graduation requirement.
courses.notes: Objective: This course will explore United States history from the Civil War to present day. This course fulfills one half of the U.S. History graduation requirement.

courses.description: This is an honors level class. American Studies will explore the establishment of the United States of America and move from the colonies through the Cold War. American Studies begins with the colonial foundations of the United States and explores the government structure and functions written in the Constitution. The development of the nation and the political, social, and economic factors that led to the Civil War are addressed. Industrialization, urbanization, and the accompanying issues are examined. This class fulfills the U.S. History graduation requirement. Civics will also be covered as part of this course.
courses.prerequisites: Teacher recommendation
courses.fulfills_text: This class fulfills the U.S. History graduation requirement.
courses.notes: Objective: This interdisciplinary course pairing meets during two blocks, one with an English teacher and one with a Global Studies teacher, who work together to blend the curriculum and skills from both departments. The pace of this class is designed to prepare students for AP Language and Composition and AP U.S. History.

courses.description: This course will cover events in U.S. History from the earliest human settlement to the present day. It is designed to make demands similar to those of an introductory college course in U.S. history. Students will strengthen their reading, writing, and critical thinking skills, and analyze a variety of historical perspectives through the use of both primary and secondary sources. This course is necessarily fast-paced; students will be required to complete a considerable amount of work outside of class. All students are required to take the AP exam. Failure to successfully complete the summer work will lead to course withdrawal.
courses.prerequisites: American Studies or U.S. History I and II, Teacher recommendation, Summer work
courses.notes: Objective: Prepare students to successfully complete the AP U.S. History exam

courses.description: The course focuses on basic principles concerning production, consumption, and distribution and services in the United States and a comparison with those in other countries around the world. Concepts and topics studied include scarcity, exchange and markets, the national economy, and the global economy.
courses.notes: Objective: This course will provide students with an understanding of economic principles, systems, and activities, in order to fully participate as a citizen in the American free enterprise system.

courses.description: This is a course on how markets work, including human behavior in relation to economics, and working to develop better financial skills. Key concepts introduced include the role of scarcity and choice, incentives and competition, and the law of supply and demand.
courses.prerequisites: Macroeconomics
courses.notes: Objective: This course will provide students with an understanding of economic principles, systems, and activities, in order to fully participate as a citizen in the American free enterprise system.

courses.description: We will examine and analyze current events. Also, we will touch upon a wide array of issues including conflict, climate change, politics, nuclear disarmament, and human rights. This class will require students to engage in discussion, and examine how government policies and events impact individuals.
courses.prerequisites: U.S. History
courses.notes: Objective: Students will develop an understanding of events that are shaping the world in which they live, engage in classroom discussions, and demonstrate critical thinking skills.

courses.description: The American legal system can appear complex and confusing. In this class students will examine our legal frameworks and explore topics including civil liberties and civil rights. Students will discuss subjects including discrimination, crime and punishment, the rules of war, and the environment.
courses.prerequisites: Global Studies, American Studies or U.S. History
courses.notes: Objective: Students will learn about the American legal system, and our individual roles and responsibilities.

courses.description: This course explores the foundations and functions of the U.S. American political system to prepare students for democratic engagement. Students will study the U.S. Constitution, the separation of powers among the three branches of government, and the landmark Supreme Court cases that define our civil liberties. Students will practice analyzing public policy, media bias, and movement strategy.
courses.notes: Objective: To equip students with the knowledge and skills to engage in the democratic process, including an understanding of the structure of our government and the historical context of its operation.

courses.description: This class counts as an general elective credit and does not count towards Global Citizenship credits required for graduation. We will engage with social justice movements throughout history and from around the world. Students will build a foundation for understanding the important issues of our time by studying what issues these movements were concerned with, what solutions they struggled for, what strategies they employed, and to what degree they were successful. Students will also examine their own social identities, values, and behaviors, as well as those of their community, exploring past movements and current events.
courses.credits_text: Half year (0.5 Credit) and students can talk both to earn 1 Credit
courses.prerequisites: U.S. History.
courses.fulfills_text: This class counts as an general elective credit and does not count towards Global Citizenship credits required for graduation.
courses.notes: Objective: Students will explore the ability to establish the skills to assert their own voices and intervene in current events.; Length/credit as printed: Half year (0.5 Credit) and students can talk both to earn 1 Credit; Catalog lists "Student Voice I and II" as one entry with a shared description

courses.description: The French department focuses on helping students acquire language through rich input using storytelling about high-interest topics or cultural readings and videos. At the French I level, input is provided in basic French through presentations, co-created stories, short readings, and narrated videos. Students practice their interpretive (reading and listening) skills on short assessments and, to a lesser degree, write about very familiar topics. In this course, we also briefly cover some regular verbs and grammar basics, but that is not the focus of the course. The course is conducted in simple, repetitive French, with English used to check for understanding. At the end of the year, students will be able to identify the main idea and details, when reading and listening in French, on familiar topics. When writing in French, students will be able to use limited, repetitive words and phrases, and occasional longer sentences, to identify common objects and actions as well as to provide basic information.
courses.notes: Objective: Students will be able to greet someone and socialize at an elementary level, as well as express themselves in very basic written language.

courses.description: This course builds upon students’ previously acquired language skills through rich input using storytelling, informational texts, and narrated videos on a variety of topics. The primary focus of the course is helping students develop their interpretive (reading and listening) skills in French, though students will also frequently practice writing about very familiar topics. Students will learn regular verbs, the immediate future tense, as well as other aspects of the French language, but this is not the focus of the course. The course is conducted in simple, repetitive French on a variety of topics, with English used to check for understanding. At the end of the year, students will be able to identify the main idea and details, when reading and listening in French, on familiar topics. When writing in French, students can use familiar words and phrases, with some elaboration, about familiar topics. Students will also be able to write longer texts in French by combining words and phrases to create original sentences.
courses.prerequisites: French I or demonstrated proficiency
courses.notes: Objective: To increase proficiency in writing and speaking while increasing practical vocabulary. Students will be able to communicate at a higher level about daily life. This will include the ability to narrate past and future events.

courses.description: At the French III level, students will still focus on building language skills through rich input using storytelling, informational texts, and narrated videos on a variety of topics, but they will also begin to interpret information about current events in French-speaking countries and across the world. Additionally, after two years of input in the language, students will naturally be able to produce more language independently when writing or speaking in French. Students will demonstrate the ability to interpret (read and listen to) texts in both the present and past tenses, and we will cover the foundations of the past tenses in French, though grammar is not the focus of this course. At the end of the year, students will be able to identify the main idea and details, when listening and reading in French, on a variety of topics. When writing and speaking in French, students will be able to use a variety of words and phrases, with some elaboration, on familiar topics. They can express themselves by connecting strings of sentences and creating original sentences and are easily understood.
courses.prerequisites: French II or demonstrated proficiency
courses.notes: Objective: To increase proficiency in writing, reading, speaking, and listening in the target language while increasing practical vocabulary; to allow students to explore multiple French cultural topics.

courses.description: In this course, students continue to build French skills by reading authentic texts, exploring cultural topics through storytelling, and increasing their knowledge of the grammatical structures of the language. Students will be comfortable expressing themselves in writing and speaking in a variety of tenses as well as in the subjunctive mood. At the end of the year, students will be able to identify the main idea and details, when listening and reading in French, on a wide variety of topics. When writing and speaking, students will be comfortable using expanded vocabulary on a variety of topics and will be able to provide details to elaborate. Students will describe and explain in French using original sentences and strings of sentences with connector words.
courses.prerequisites: French III or demonstrated proficiency
courses.notes: Objective: Continue to increase proficiency in writing, reading, speaking, and listening in the target language, and explore additional French cultural topics.

courses.description: The Spanish department helps students acquire language through rich input using storytelling about high-interest topics or cultural readings and videos. At the Spanish 1 level, input is provided in basic Spanish through presentations, co-created stories, short readings, and narrated videos. Students practice their interpretive (reading and listening) skills on short assessments and, to a lesser degree, write about very familiar topics. We also briefly cover some regular verbs and grammar basics, but that is not the focus of the course. The course is conducted in simple, repetitive Spanish, with English used to check for understanding. At the end of the year, students will be able to identify the main idea and details, when reading and listening in Spanish, on familiar topics. When writing, students will be able to use limited, repetitive words and phrases, and occasional longer sentences, to identify common objects and actions as well as to provide basic information.
courses.notes: Objective: To be able to recognize familiar words and phrases in Spanish and present information on familiar topics using practiced words and phrases.

courses.description: This course builds upon students’ previously acquired language skills through rich input using storytelling, informational texts, and narrated videos on a variety of topics. The primary focus of the course is developing students’ interpretive (reading and listening) skills in Spanish, though students will also frequently practice writing about very familiar topics. Students will learn regular verbs, the immediate future tense, and other aspects of the Spanish language, but grammar is not the focus of the course. The course is conducted in simple, repetitive Spanish on a variety of topics, with English used to check for understanding. At the end of the year, students will be able to identify the main idea and details, when reading and listening in Spanish, on familiar topics. When writing, students will be able to use familiar words and phrases, with some elaboration, about familiar topics. Students will also be able to produce more written Spanish by combining words and phrases.
courses.prerequisites: Spanish I or demonstrated proficiency
courses.notes: Objective: To be able to understand the main idea and some details when reading in Spanish and present basic information about everyday topics using simple sentences.

courses.description: At the Spanish 3 level, students will still focus on building language skills through rich input using storytelling, informational texts, and narrated videos on a variety of topics, but they will also begin to interpret information about current events in Spanish-speaking countries and across the world. Additionally, after two years of input in the language, students will naturally be able to produce more language independently when writing or speaking in Spanish. Students will demonstrate the ability to interpret (read and listen to) texts in both the present and past tenses, and we will cover the foundations of the past tenses in Spanish, though grammar is not the focus of this course. At the end of the year, students will be able to identify the main idea and details, when listening and reading in Spanish, on a variety of topics. When writing and speaking in Spanish, students will be able to use a variety of words and phrases, with some elaboration, on familiar topics. They can express themselves by connecting strings of sentences, creating original sentences, and they are easily understood by someone used to a language learner.
courses.prerequisites: Spanish II or demonstrated proficiency
courses.notes: Objective: To be able to understand the main idea and details when reading texts in Spanish and present information on a variety of familiar topics using connected sentences.

courses.description: In this course, students continue to build Spanish skills by reading authentic texts, exploring cultural topics through storytelling, and increasing their knowledge of the grammatical structures of the language. Though grammar is still not the primary focus of this class, students will be comfortable expressing themselves in writing and speaking in a variety of tenses as well as in the subjunctive mood. A primary focus of the course will be discussing Spanish current events and watching an authentic Spanish telenovela. At the end of the year, students will be able to identify the main idea and details, when listening and reading in Spanish, on a wide variety of topics. When writing and speaking, students will be comfortable using expanded vocabulary on a variety of topics and will be able to provide details to elaborate. Students will describe and explain in Spanish using original sentences and strings of sentences with connector words.
courses.prerequisites: Spanish III or demonstrated proficiency
courses.notes: Objective: To be able to understand the main idea and details when reading texts in Spanish and present information on a variety of familiar topics using connected sentences with supporting details and elaboration.

courses.description: In this course, students continue to build Spanish skills by reading authentic texts, exploring cultural topics through storytelling, and increasing their knowledge of the grammatical structures of the language. Students will be comfortable expressing themselves in writing and speaking in a variety of tenses as well as in the subjunctive mood. A primary focus of the course will be discussing Spanish current events and watching a variety of authentic Spanish media. At the end of the year, students will be able to identify the main idea and details, when listening and reading in Spanish, on a wide variety of topics. When writing and speaking, students will be comfortable using expanded vocabulary on a variety of familiar and unfamiliar topics and will be able to provide details to elaborate. Students will describe and explain in Spanish using original sentences and strings of sentences with connector words.
courses.prerequisites: Spanish IV or demonstrated proficiency
courses.notes: Objective: To be able to understand the main idea and details when reading texts in Spanish and present information on a variety of familiar and unfamiliar topics using connected sentences with supporting details and elaboration.

courses.course_name: Pixel and Vector: Introduction to Digital Illustration and Graphic Design
courses.description: Students will explore digital drawing, image editing, typography, layout design, branding, and visual storytelling using industry-standard software and digital tools. Throughout the course, students will create original illustrations, logos, posters, social media graphics, and other design projects while learning the principles of design such as color theory, composition, contrast, balance, and hierarchy. Emphasis is placed on creative problem-solving, developing a personal style, and understanding how design communicates ideas and messages to specific audiences. Students will build a portfolio of digital work suitable for college applications or future careers in art, design, marketing, and media.
courses.notes: Objective: Students will analyze and apply elements and principles of design to produce effective digital illustrations, logos, and visual communication projects using industry-standard software.

courses.course_name: Get Fired Up! Introduction to Sculpture and Ceramics
courses.description: Sculpture & Ceramics is a studio course that introduces students to three-dimensional art and design. Students will explore sculptural techniques using a variety of materials, including clay, wire, plaster, found objects, and mixed media. Emphasis is placed on form, texture, balance, proportion, and craftsmanship. In the ceramics portion of the course, students will learn fundamental hand-building techniques such as pinch, coil, and slab construction, as well as an introduction to the pottery wheel. Students will explore surface design, glazing techniques, and the firing process while developing both functional and expressive works of art. Throughout the course, students will strengthen problem-solving skills, creative thinking, and artistic voice while building a portfolio of finished pieces. No prior experience is required—just a willingness to experiment, get a little messy, and think in three dimensions.
courses.notes: Objective: Students will develop foundational skills in three-dimensional design by creating original sculptures and ceramic works that demonstrate craftsmanship, creativity, and understanding of form and structure.

courses.course_name: Capture This! A Look at Digital Photography and Video Production
courses.description: This course introduces students to the art and technology of digital photography and video production. Students will learn how to use digital cameras and editing software to capture, enhance, and produce compelling visual stories. Emphasis is placed on composition, lighting, camera settings, storytelling, and visual communication. Students will explore photography techniques such as portraiture, landscape, action, and conceptual photography, while also learning the fundamentals of videography including shot composition, camera movement, audio recording, and basic video editing. Through individual and collaborative projects, students will create original photo series, short films, and multimedia pieces. Throughout the course, students will develop technical skills, creative confidence, and critical thinking while building a portfolio of digital work suitable for college, career pathways, or personal creative growth.
courses.notes: Objective: Students will develop foundational skills in digital photography and video production by applying composition, lighting, editing, and storytelling techniques to create original visual media projects.

courses.course_name: Brush and Beyond: The Basics of Drawing and Painting
courses.description: This course provides students with a comprehensive introduction to a wide range of drawing and painting media, techniques, and creative processes. Through structured studio experiences and exploratory projects, students will build foundational skills in observation, composition, color theory, shading, perspective, and mark-making. Emphasis will be placed on both technical development and personal expression. Students will deepen their understanding of the elements and principles of design such as line, value, color, texture, balance, contrast, and emphasis while creating original works that communicate their own individualized narrative. Projects will encourage experimentation, creative risk-taking, and the development of a unique artistic voice. Media explored will include pencil, colored pencil, charcoal, pastel, oil pastel, ink, acrylic paint, acrylic paint markers, watercolor, watercolor pencils, tempera, and ink/gouache.
courses.notes: Objective: Students will explore and experiment with a variety of drawing and painting techniques while developing a strong understanding of the fundamental elements and principles of design. Students will practice composition, color, line, texture, and value to create expressive, visually compelling artwork that communicates ideas and personal creativity.

courses.course_name: Press & Impress: Basics of Printmaking Techniques
courses.description: This course introduces students to the foundational techniques, tools, and processes of traditional and contemporary printmaking. Students will gain experience with a variety of print media while developing craftsmanship, problem-solving skills, and creative expression. Through guided instruction as well as independent projects, students will explore image development, carving and inking techniques, registration, layering, and editioning. Techniques explored will include linocut printing, woodcut printing, monoprinting, screenprinting, and introductory etching processes. Students will learn safe studio practices, proper tool use, and print studio procedures while producing a body of original work that demonstrates both technical skill and creative growth.
courses.notes: Objective: Students will experiment with a variety of printmaking techniques while developing an understanding of the fundamental elements and principles of design. Through studio practice, students will explore composition, contrast, texture, balance, and repetition as they create original prints that demonstrate both technical skill and creative expression.

courses.course_name: Sketch to Screen: Exploration of Illustration and Animation
courses.description: This dynamic course introduces students to the creative process of transforming drawings into animated visuals. Students will explore foundational illustration techniques, character design, storyboarding, and basic animation principles. Through hands-on projects, students will experiment with both traditional and digital tools to develop original characters, short visual narratives, and simple animations. The course emphasizes creativity, visual storytelling, and problem-solving while helping students build confidence in their artistic voice and technical skills.
courses.notes: Objective: Students will develop foundational skills in illustration and animation by learning to create original characters, plan visual stories through storyboards, and produce short animated sequences. By the end of the course, students will demonstrate an understanding of basic animation principles, visual storytelling techniques, and the process of moving from concept sketch to finished screen-based work.

courses.course_name: Portfolio Development: Advanced Level Studio Art
courses.description: This portfolio-building course provides students with a personalized studio experience focused on individual artistic growth. Through a structured goal-setting process, students will develop a course of study aligned with their interests, strengths, and future aspirations. Students will create original work that demonstrates technical skill, creative problem-solving, and conceptual development while building a cohesive digital portfolio. Those considering art-related college programs or careers will also conduct research into their chosen field, including portfolio requirements and career pathways.
courses.prerequisites: 2 courses completed and permission from the art teacher
courses.notes: Objective: Students will pursue individualized art projects that reflect their personal interests, strengths, and creative goals while developing technical skills and artistic voice. Students will build and refine a cohesive portfolio that demonstrates growth, originality, and readiness for college programs and/or creative career pathways.; Length/credit as printed: Half year (0.5 - 1 Credit)

courses.description: Concert Choir builds on the foundation developed through the elementary and middle school chorus programs. Prior choir experience is not required. Students collaborate and become part of our musical community through solo & ensemble performances, festivals, concerts and travel experiences. Some performances outside of the school day are a required part of the curriculum. Students can take this course more than once for credit.
courses.notes: Objective: Develop successful habits of work through the pursuit of music literacy.

courses.description: Concert Band builds on the foundation developed through the 5th-8th grade band programs. Students collaborate and become part of our musical community through solo and ensemble performances, festivals, concerts and travel experiences. Some performances outside of the school day are a required part of the curriculum. Students without instruments can contact the director for information regarding the use of a school-owned instrument. Students can take this course more than once for credit.
courses.prerequisites: Prior concert band experience or instructor approval is required. Students who have not been in band before must first consult with the teacher.
courses.notes: Objective: Develop successful habits of work through the pursuit of music literacy.

courses.description: This college level course introduces the student to musicianship, theory, musical materials, and procedures. It integrates aspects of melody, harmony, texture, rhythm, form, and musical analysis, elementary composition and, to some extent, history and style. Musicianship skills such as dictation and other listening skills, sight singing, and keyboard harmony are an important part of the theory course. The student’s ability to read and write musical notation is fundamental to such a course. It is also assumed that the student has acquired at least moderate performance skills in voice or on an instrument.
courses.prerequisites: Recommendation of music directors
courses.notes: Objective: Develop a student’s ability to recognize, understand, and describe the basic materials and processes of music that are heard or presented in a score.

courses.description: This course provides skill training in various 2D and 3D software and encourages the student to develop the visualization skills needed to be successful in interpreting technical communications. Students contemplating a career in any engineering, architectural, mechanical or construction field will benefit from this course as they will be required to take a similar course during their first year in college or technical school.
courses.prerequisites: Algebra I or concurrent enrollment
courses.notes: Objective: Students will learn to use professional level 2D and 3D software to do computer drafting and 3-D modeling.

courses.description: Students will gain hands-on experience working on small engines, automobiles, and agricultural machinery. Students will learn the basics of engine operation and vehicle maintenance, as well as general knowledge applicable to all machine systems. Students will be introduced to basic welding techniques. The course is excellent preparation for anyone interested in attending a high school technical program or doing work on their own vehicles.
courses.notes: Objective: To develop an understanding of how mechanical systems work and what is required to repair and build them.

courses.description: This is an introductory course in working with wood, using hand and power tools. Students will develop competency in the safe use of hand and power tools, and will gain an understanding of the design requirements of simple wood projects. This course will be extremely useful for students considering engineering or scientific research fields. Woodworking is also a valuable life skill enabling the mastering of applied math.
courses.notes: Objective: Students will become competent in the skills necessary to design and build basic basic woodworking projects using hand and power tools safely.

courses.description: Students work to build on the skills learned in Woodworking I in order to gain an understanding of the design and engineering requirements of more complicated wood projects.
courses.prerequisites: Woodworking I
courses.notes: Objective: Students will build on skills learned in Woodworking I to build more complicated projects.

courses.description: Vermont requires that students have six hours of front seat (driving) and six hours of back seat time (observing other students). Students learn the maneuvers required on the Vermont Road Test while driving on country roads, city streets and the interstate. Students are also exposed to as many bad weather driving conditions as possible. Classroom instruction includes such topics as attitude and social responsibility, laws related to driving, safe driving procedures, insurance and financial responsibility, effects of alcohol and other drugs, minimizing the effect of automobiles on the environment, purchasing and financing an automobile, and other related topics. Technological changes, such as anti-locking brakes, are discussed, and students are made aware of changes in driving methods brought about by technology. Upon successful completion of both classroom and driving phases of the course, the student receives a Vermont Driver Education Certificate, needed to obtain a license before age 18. Student and instructor will schedule mutually agreeable driving times.
courses.credits_text: Trimester (0.5 credit) - The course takes approximately two months to complete
courses.prerequisites: Students must be at least 15 years old and possess a VT Learner’s Permit by the first day of class. Also, students must sign up through the vendor’s website. Students are prioritized by age when populating classes.
courses.notes: Objective: To become aware of the importance of the social responsibility needed for safe driving, and to acquire the knowledge and skills needed to be ready for licensing.; Length/credit as printed: Trimester (0.5 credit) - The course takes approximately two months to complete

courses.description: Physical Education will teach the tools needed in order to live a healthy and active lifestyle. Emphasis shall be placed on personal, physical, and social development. Students will be taught the skills needed to participate in a variety of units from fitness to ultimate Frisbee. Students will be assessed on participation, effort, as well as state physical fitness testing. Assessment will be based on the district proficiency based graduation requirements.
courses.notes: Objective: Develop the skills, understanding, and desire to participate in physical activities long after high school and maintain a healthy, active lifestyle.; Catalog lists "Physical Education I and II" as one entry with a shared description

courses.description: This is an upper level class designed for students who are serious about fitness. Fitness is more physically demanding than P.E. class. Flexibility, cardiovascular endurance, muscle strength, muscle endurance and body composition are the five components of fitness and will be worked on in class. Students will learn exciting ways to work out and the importance of building muscle and increasing cardiovascular endurance.
courses.prerequisites: Physical Education
courses.notes: Objective: To develop the skills needed to be successful and comfortable in a fitness center. Students will understand the link between exercise and being healthy.

courses.description: This class provides students with opportunities to develop leadership, fitness knowledge, and physical competence while taking an active role in guiding the class experience. Students will be responsible for helping plan, lead, and participate in a variety of physical activities, workouts, and recreational games throughout the semester. Emphasis is placed on “student led”, leadership, teamwork, sportsmanship, and personal responsibility for maintaining an active and healthy lifestyle.
courses.prerequisites: Physical Education
courses.notes: Objective: This class is designed to allow students who have taken a P.E. or Fitness class as a prerequisite, to be able to push beyond their limits and be in a more competitive group, and allows them to be in charge of the class.; Catalog lists "Advanced Physical Education I and II" as one entry with a shared description
